concept.title: Set many properties with a shorthand
concept.shortdesc: A shorthand property sets several properties in one declaration. Use it to write less CSS, and know what it does to the properties you leave out.

conbody.p: The properties that a shorthand sets are its longhands. The shorthand margin, for example, sets the four longhands margin-top, margin-right, margin-bottom and margin-left. The number of values you write decides how they are shared:

One value is for all four sides. Two values are for top and bottom, then right and left. Three values are for top, right and left, then bottom. Four values go clockwise from the top: top, right, bottom, left.
The shorthands border, background, font, padding and many others work in the same way, each with its own order of values. The topics , , and explain the shorthands of their properties.

section.title: A shorthand resets what you leave out
section.p: A shorthand always sets all its longhands. The longhands that you do not write get their initial value, and that can replace a value that an earlier rule gave:
The second rule sets background-image to none too, so the title has a plain yellow background. Write the longhand after the shorthand when you need both.

section.title: Shorthands in the cascade
section.p: CSSMedia replaces a shorthand with its longhands at the position of the declaration. They compete with the other declarations like longhands that you wrote one by one:
In the chapter, the shorthand comes later, so the left margin is 1em. In the title, the longhand comes later, so the left margin is 2em and the other margins are 1em.

If you write !important after a shorthand, all its longhands are important. A declaration with a value that is not valid for the shorthand sets none of its longhands, and the earlier declarations stay. If you write a keyword such as inherit as the whole value of a shorthand, it applies to every longhand:

section.title: The shorthand for everything
section.p: The property all is a shorthand for all the properties. Inherit, reset and roll back values explains it.
